Surah al-Fatihah: An Overview

A Muslim recites this short surah, consisting of seven verses, at least seventeen times a day and night, and when he prays the Sunnah prayers the number doubles. And if he prays voluntary prayers (nawafil) besides the obligatory and Sunnah prayers, he recites it countless times. A prayer is not valid without the recitation of this surah. In a sound hadith, Hadrat Ubadah ibn al-Samit (raa) narrates from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Fatihah."

This surah contains the lofty principles of Islamic belief, the fundamental axioms of the Islamic worldview, and extremely important basic guidance for the human intellect and human concerns. This is why Allah has made the recitation of this surah obligatory in every rak'ah of the prayer, and a prayer in which this surah is not recited has been declared invalid.

The surah begins with "Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim" (﷽). Among the jurists there is a difference of opinion as to whether this is a verse of every surah or a verse of the whole Qur'an, and whether each surah is begun with it only at the time of recitation. However, the well-established view is that the Bismillah is a verse of Surah al-Fatihah, and only by counting it is the number of verses of Surah al-Fatihah seven. In the Qur'an it is stated: ﴿And We have given you seven of the oft-repeated (verses) and the great Qur'an﴾ (al-Hijr: 87). The meaning of this verse has one opinion that it refers to Surah al-Fatihah, because it has seven verses, and it is called "al-mathani" because it is repeated again and again in the prayer.

Beginning with the Bismillah is among the etiquettes which Allah taught His Prophet (ﷺ) at the commencement of revelation: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ (al-Alaq: 1). It is among the etiquettes that conform to the fundamental belief of the Islamic worldview. Allah says: ﴿He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden﴾ (al-Hadid: 3). Allah alone possesses true and real existence, and all other beings derive their existence from Him. Everything begins from Him, therefore a Muslim begins every beginning and every movement in His name.

The attributes of Allah, al-Rahman and al-Rahim, which are mentioned at the beginning, encompass all the aspects of mercy. These two may be used together only for Allah, and al-Rahman alone may also be used only for Allah. It is permissible to call a human being "rahim" other than Allah, but according to Islamic belief it is not permissible to call a servant "Rahman." It is preferable to use both these attributes together for Allah, that is, "Rahman wa Rahim." Although there is a difference of opinion as to which of these two words has the broader meaning, in the shade of the Qur'an we are not much interested in such discussions. Rather, the distinguishing feature of these two is that they together contain all the meanings, all the dimensions and all the breadth of mercy. Beginning speech with the Bismillah, which contains the meanings of Allah's greatness and oneness, is the first principle of the Islamic worldview; and the encompassing within the two attributes Rahman and Rahim of all the meanings, all the conditions and all the breadth of mercy is the second golden principle of the Islamic worldview, through which the correct nature of the relationship between a servant and his Allah is expressed.

After beginning with *Bismillah al-Rahman al-Raheem*, the human being now turns towards his Lord, praises Him, and proclaims His universal lordship over the whole creation. ﴿Al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin﴾, "Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all the worlds." The consciousness of praising Allah is what surges in the heart of the believer whenever Allah's name is mentioned, and the believer's heart is filled with it, because human existence itself, at its very beginning, is one of the countless blessings and bounties. This becomes a stirring force for the feelings of praise and glorification of Allah in the heart of the believer.

Allah's blessings come at every step, every moment, continuously and in abundance, and they benefit all of Allah's creatures, and especially this "human being." Therefore, beginning every task with the praise of Allah, and ending every task with His praise and glorification, is one of the important principles of the Islamic conception of life. ﴿Wa huwa Allahu la ilaha illa huwa, lahu al-hamdu fi al-ula wa al-akhirah﴾, "And He is Allah; there is no god but He. To Him belongs praise in the first and in the last." Note the kindness and generosity of Allah towards such a servant: when he utters "Alhamdulillah" with his tongue, Allah writes down for him a good deed that outweighs all other good deeds. In a hadith narrated by Hadrat Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) in Ibn Majah, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A servant praised Allah and said: *Ya Rabbi, laka al-hamdu kama yanbaghi li jalali wajhika wa 'azimi sultanika*," meaning, "O Allah, to You is praise befitting the majesty of Your Face and the greatness of Your sovereignty."

"The angels were perplexed in this matter and could not decide how to record it. So they came into the presence of Allah and submitted: 'O our Lord! Your servant has said something that we do not understand how to record.' Although Allah knew what the servant had said, He asked the angels: 'What did My servant say?' The angels replied: 'He said, "O Allah, to You is praise that befits the majesty and glory of Your Face and the greatness of Your sovereignty."' Then Allah commanded them to write it exactly as My servant said it. On the Day of Judgment he will meet Me, and I Myself will reward him."

In short, turning to Allah with His praise is the consciousness of the believer which surges in the heart of the believer as soon as Allah's name comes upon the tongue. The second part of this verse, *Rabb al-'Alamin*, is also a fundamental principle of the Islamic conception of life. The universal and absolute lordship (*rububiyyah*) of Allah is the foundation of all Islamic beliefs. *Rabb* refers to the one who is the owner and the disposer of affairs, and in the Arabic language this word is also used for the leader who exercises control over something for the sake of its reform and training. The disposal and nurturing for reform and training encompasses all worlds and all creatures. Allah did not create creatures so that they would be left aimlessly, but Allah alone is the disposer of this universe and its reformer. He oversees it and continuously sustains it. The care of all worlds and all creatures is carried out under the supervision of the *Rabb al-'Alamin*. The connection between the Creator and the creation is maintained at every moment, in every state, and it continuously flows.

This explanation and clarification of the complete and all-encompassing doctrine of Tawhid (Oneness of Allah) draws a clear distinction between it and that confused thinking. Sometimes it happens, and it is still happening, that people acknowledge the One God and the Creator of the universe, yet in addition to that they also believe in multiple deities and lords, and they accept those deities and lords as rulers in their lives. Although at first glance this belief appears extremely ridiculous, the reality is that some people held this belief and still do. The Qur'an has described the belief that some polytheists held about their deities and lords:

﴿Ma na'buduhum illa liyuqarribuna ilaa Allahi zulfa﴾ (Az-Zumar 39:3), "We worship them only so that they may bring us near to Allah in closeness." This is similar to what was said about the People of the Book: ﴿Ittakhadhu ahbarahum wa ruhbanahum arbaban min dun Allah﴾ (At-Tawbah 9:31), "They have taken their scholars and their monks as lords besides Allah." At the time of the revelation of the Qur'an, the condition of the polytheists of Arabia was that, alongside the great deities, they also believed in smaller lords, and according to their thinking these smaller lords were those who performed the function of divinity alongside the great gods.

Therefore, in this context, stating universal lordship and making it general and inclusive of all worlds has the purpose of drawing a clear line between the intellectual disorder of *Jahiliyyah* (the age of ignorance) and the ideological harmony of Islam. This is so that the whole universe and all people turn towards One Allah alone, affirm His absolute sovereignty, cast off from their necks the yoke of slavery to multiple lords, and be freed from the intellectual confusion and anxiety in which they keep becoming entangled by believing in countless gods. In this way, the conscience of Allah's creatures becomes content under the constant supervision of Allah and the enduring lordship, a lordship that is never interrupted, whose continuity is established and flowing forever and ever.

Let it be remembered that this is not the kind of lordship whose concept was presented by Aristotle, who said that Allah created this universe and then left it as it is. He says: "What concern is it of Allah to think about things lower than Himself? He thinks only about His own essence." This opinion belongs to a man who is regarded as a great philosopher, whose philosophy is considered solid, whose intellect is accepted as profound, and who is acknowledged as a genius.

When the teachings of Islam began, the world possessed a vast store of beliefs, conceptions, thoughts, superstitions, philosophies and traditions, in which there was no distinction between truth and falsehood. There was no separation between the genuine and the counterfeit. Superstitions had become part of religion. Philosophies and beliefs were a heap of illusions and superstitions, and the human conscience was buried under the layered accumulation of these illusions and traditions, and, deprived of certainty, it was groping in the dark abyss of doubt and conjecture.

What was this bewilderment and confusion in which it found neither peace nor any ray of the light of guidance? It was simply the concept of divinity of that time. The meaning of *Ilah al-'Alamin*, His attributes, His relationship with creation, and such issues, especially the true nature of the relationship between Allah and man, all the beliefs of that time were afflicted with this misguidance and error.

Before the human being could form a concept of his Allah and His attributes, and be freed from the existing turmoil, bewilderment and the heavy mass of illusions and imaginings of that time, it was not possible for his conscience to become content regarding this universe, regarding his own self, or regarding a system of life for himself, nor could he attain tranquility and peace. (Therefore, first of all, the correction of the concept of divinity and freedom from those false ideas was necessary.)

The realization of the necessity and importance of this peace and purification of beliefs cannot come to a person unless he has a thorough acquaintance with the breadth and depth of this intellectual misguidance, and has complete knowledge of how many layers of wrong beliefs and concepts, false philosophies and mistaken traditions were piled upon the hearts and minds of people when Islam came. Here we have only briefly pointed towards them. A detailed discussion will take place in those places where the Qur'an has dealt with these concepts in detail.

For these reasons, Islam first of all discussed the Islamic beliefs and the fundamental concepts of Islam in detail, and it clearly and definitively established and defined the Islamic concept regarding the essence and attributes of Allah, His relationship with creation, and the nature of the bond between creation and its Creator. That is why the foundation of the Islamic conception of life became that complete, pure and all-encompassing Tawhid, in which there was not even a trace of *shirk* (association of partners with Allah). This has been continuously clarified in the Islamic teachings. All doubts and misgivings arising about it have been eliminated. Every kind of confusion and ambiguity regarding it has been removed, and it has been purified and placed in the heart of the believer in a pure and clear form, so that he does not fall into illusion or conjecture in this matter. Islam also gave clear and unambiguous teachings about the attributes of Allah and the attribute of absolute lordship. This is because a large part of the false philosophies and baseless theories consisted of those polytheistic illusions and myths regarding the attributes of Allah, which those false philosophies had implanted in the minds and hearts of people. They had a great influence on the human conscience, and these concepts were also influencing human conduct.

Those who have only superficially studied the efforts which Islam made to make people understand the essence and attributes of Allah and the nature of His relationship with creation, and in whose explanation countless verses of the Qur'an were revealed, and who have not studied the false philosophies and polytheistic theories under whose heavy burden the human conscience was crushed, and by which all humanity was lost, will by no means be able to grasp the true reason for those efforts of the Qur'an, its extreme emphasis, repetition, detail and clarification regarding beliefs. On the contrary, the one who thoroughly studies the false theories and beliefs that were prevalent at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an will understand clearly the reality, importance and necessity of those efforts. He will be able to understand what role the doctrine of Tawhid played in the freedom of the human conscience, because it freed man from illusions, myths and the mythological concepts of many gods.

In short, the beauty of the doctrine of Tawhid, its perfection, its harmony, and the simplicity and realism of the truth expressed in it cannot be understood until a person carefully examines the false beliefs, concepts, myths and traditions that were prevalent in the world at that time, especially the reality of the Divine Being and the nature of His relationship with this world. Only after a deep study of these false ideas can it become clear that the Islamic way of life is in reality a blessing. It is a mercy for both heart and sight. Its beauty and simplicity are a divine favor, its harmony with human nature and its reasonableness, its closeness and familiarity to the human mind, and its balance and moderation: all of this is a special mercy of Allah which He bestowed upon His creation.

The attribute al-Rahman al-Rahim is repeated here in the middle of the surah as an independent verse. It encompasses every meaning, circumstance and breadth of mercy and compassion. The purpose of repeating it here is to highlight one especially distinguished aspect of Allah's universal lordship (rububiyyah), and to stir praise and gratitude (hamd wa thana) through the bond between the Creator and creation, between Allah and His nurtured servants. This bond rests on the foundation of tranquility of heart, and its strings are woven into a heart filled with love. Therefore, "al-Hamdu lillah" is in truth the voice of human nature that rises in response to Allah's boundless mercy.

The concept of Allah and Lord that Islam presents is entirely different from the concept that Greek thought presented about the Olympian (Olympic) gods. According to that concept, these hard-hearted gods pursued their servants equally in times of peace and in times of war, and kept chasing their servants like an enemy. But the Allah of the worlds (Ilah al-'Alamin) of Islam does not adopt the administrative measures for His servants that are mentioned in the distorted traditions of the Old Testament. For example, the account given about Babel in Chapter 11 of the Book of Genesis is the clearest illustration of this:

("And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech. And it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there. And they said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them thoroughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for mortar. And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth. And the LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded. And the LORD said, Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do: and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do. Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech. So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city. Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.")

Surah 1, verse 4:

"Master of the Day of Recompense" (Maliki yawmi'd-din).

In this verse is stated a fundamental and basic belief of Islam, whose effects on the whole of human life are very profound. Allah has used the word "Malik" (Master, Owner) with regard to the Day of Recompense, which indicates the highest degree of possession, dominion, disposal and authority. Yawm al-Din (the Day of Recompense) means the Day of Judgement, the Day of Recompense on the Last Day.

It should be remembered that at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an there were some people who accepted Allah as the Ilah (God), and also believed in Allah's attribute of creation, and said that it was Allah who brought this world into existence from non-existence; nevertheless, they did not believe in the Day of Recompense and reckoning. Concerning such people the Qur'an says: "And if you were to ask them, 'Who created the heavens and the earth?' they would surely say, 'Allah.'" (Az-Zumar 39:38 partial). And elsewhere it says: "They wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves, and the disbelievers say, 'This is a strange thing. When we have died and become dust, [will we be returned?] That is a far return.'" (Qaf 50:2-3)

Belief in the Last Day is one of the essential articles of faith of Islam, and its importance in creating in people's hearts and minds the sense of accountability before Allah in the Hereafter, beyond this world, is universally acknowledged. Those who believe in this creed do not become absorbed merely in acquiring the needs of this lowly world; rather, after believing in this creed, they think above worldly needs and requirements. They have no concern as to whether within this limited short life and this narrow sphere of worldly retribution they receive the full reward of their good deeds or not. Rather, the sole aim of all their goodness and all their striving in the way of Allah is the pleasure of Allah. They seek the reward of their deeds from Allah alone, whether it is received in this world or in the Hereafter. They remain content. They rely upon truth and righteousness. They hold firmly to the truth and become possessors of the wealth of certainty, breadth of heart and vision, and good character... In short, this fundamental belief is the criterion by which it is determined whether a person is merely a slave and servant of his own desires and appetites, or whether he also possesses the freedom and liberty befitting human dignity. Through this it becomes known whether, in this world, worldly values, material conceptions and ignorance hold the superiority, or whether Divine values, spiritual conceptions and the Islamic outlook on life have dominance over the logic of ignorance. Moreover, through this fundamental belief, that lofty station which Allah has chosen for His servants becomes clear, and the distinction between defective, impure and deviant conceptions of life and this lofty station of humanity also becomes evident.

Until this fundamental belief takes root in the hearts and minds of human beings, and until peace settles in people's hearts that worldly benefits and material desires are not the whole destiny of man, and until this mortal human being is convinced that there is a life to come, and that it is his duty to strive for that next world and that life, to sacrifice for it, to support truth, to cooperate in goodness, and that he will receive the reward of all these things in the Hereafter, human life cannot be established according to the Islamic system of life.

One who believes in the belief of the Hereafter and one who denies it can by no means be equal in morality, consciousness, thought and action. Therefore, these two groups are separate species of Allah's creation. These two have different natures, and in this world their conduct can by no means be the same, nor in the Hereafter can they both deserve the same kind of recompense. Therefore, this belief becomes the cause of a clear distinction between the two.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 1, verse 5:

﴿Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'een﴾ "We worship You alone, and from You alone we seek help." This too is a fundamental principle, and it is the logical outcome of the beliefs mentioned before it. No one other than Allah is worthy of worship and servitude, and no one is worthy of being asked for help. This belief also draws a clear line between truth and falsehood in this field. From it one learns what complete freedom from every kind of bondage truly is, and what the reality of one human being's enslavement to another is. This principle is in essence a great public proclamation that human beings must be granted complete and full freedom. Freedom from following superstitions and myths, freedom from being bound to corrupt customs and manners, and freedom from submission to a false system of life: when worship belongs to One Allah alone and help is sought from One Allah alone, the human conscience attains freedom from other human beings, from jahili (ignorant) systems of life, and from the shackles of customs and traditions. Along with this, the view of a Muslim should be made clear regarding superstitions and myths, religious mythology, and cosmic forces (physical powers).

From the viewpoint of a Muslim, human power and authority are of two kinds. One is that power which is founded upon guidance and the straight path and which submits to the Islamic system of life. Regarding this, the policy of a Muslim is that he assists and supports it in goodness, truth and reformative works, and considers this his duty. The second is the jahili power, which has strayed from the straight path and does not submit to the Islamic system of life. Regarding this, the policy of a Muslim is that he opposes it, fights against it, and, by eliminating it, helps establish in its place the correct power and authority.

Remember! A Muslim should not be disturbed by the outward bulk and grandeur of jahili power, because for a Muslim the true source of power is the Divine Being. Jahiliyyah has cut itself off from this true source of power, which continuously and perpetually supplies strength to human beings. You see that when some great body among the celestial bodies separates from a blazing star, it is not long before it grows cold and dies out. Its light becomes dim and its heat ends, even though its outward body may be magnificent. But on the contrary, if even a insignificant particle is connected to the true source of its power and light, it continuously receives heat and light from it, and the situation is: ﴿Kam min fi'atin qaleelatin ghalabat fi'atan katheeratan bi-idhnillah﴾ "How often has a small company overcome a large company by the permission of Allah" (Al-Baqarah: 249).

As for physical power, a believer's relationship with it is one of knowledge, understanding, friendship and harmony; it is not a relationship of fear and enmity. This is because both human and natural powers are the outcome of one origin and one will; that is, they are subject to the will of the Lord, and both are subdued and overpowered before the decrees of the Creator of the universe. Between them there is complete harmony and full cooperation. They move alike, and the direction of their movement is also one.

It is the belief and worldview of a Muslim that teaches him that Allah Almighty created this universe precisely so that the believer may be its friend, helper and supporter, and this friendship can be realized in this way: a believer reflects upon the universe, becomes acquainted with it, cooperates with it, and, together with this universe, turns his face toward his Lord. Although apparently at times physical powers cause harm to a human being, the reason is that the human being errs in understanding them; he does not reflect deeply upon them, and he forgets that true power which is sustaining this whole universe.

The Western heirs of Roman jahiliyyah have come to have a sort of fashion of describing the use of physical powers with the words "conquest of nature." This expression clearly shows that the bond of this jahiliyyah with the Lord of the universe has been severed, and it has no connection with that spirit of the universe which is responding labbaik to Allah. As for the Muslim whose heart is attached to the Most Merciful and Most Compassionate, and who is also connected to the universe in whose glorification and declaration of Allah's oneness, the Lord of all the worlds, every power is absorbed, he believes that apart from wrath and oppression there is another kind of relationship with the universe. His faith is that Allah is the Creator of this universe. It is He who created this whole universe and all its powers, and for it He established the order of the laws of nature, so that all these powers, within its bounds, fulfill those purposes which are desired by Allah. Allah created this universe solely for the sake of man. Then Allah Almighty granted man the facility to understand its laws and regulations and to discover its secrets. Whenever he discovers some new secret of these mysteries, it is his duty to thank Allah Almighty, for it is Allah who has subjected the universe to him. By himself, it is beyond the power of man to do this duty of thanking Allah; it is Allah who has subjected this universe to him. By himself, man had no ability to subdue and overpower this universe. ﴿Sakhkhara lakum ma fil-ard﴾ "He has subjected to you whatever is in the earth" (Al-Jathiyah: 13).

As a result of this concept, a believer's perception and awareness regarding these cosmic forces is free from every kind of superstition and myth. There are no veils of fear and dread between him and these cosmic forces. He believes only in the One God, worships only the One God, and seeks help only from the Unique Lord. As for these physical powers, according to his conception of the universe, they too are a part of Allah's creation. He reflects upon them, takes interest in them, and strives to discover their secrets; in response, these creative forces become his helpers and open their secrets before him, and he lives with these forces a peaceful, affectionate, sincere life, like a sincere friend and familiar companion. Raising his gaze toward Mount Uhud, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said beautifully: "This is a mountain, and it loves us, and we love it." These words express the reality that the first Muslim, the Prophet (ﷺ), held in his heart such esteem and love even for a mountain, the most solid form of this universe, and that he had such attachment to it.

After these fundamental points of the Islamic worldview, and after this clarification that in worship and seeking help a Muslim must turn only to Allah Almighty, the practical application of these matters now begins. Through supplication and humble entreaty, the servant of God now turns toward Allah Almighty, and this supplication too is a fundamental supplication which is in complete harmony and conformity with the fundamental atmosphere of this surah and its overall temperament.

"Guide us to the straight path."

"Guide us to the straight path." That is, grant us the ability to understand the path that is straight and that leads to the intended destination. And after understanding it, grant us steadfastness upon it. For recognition of the truth, and then steadfastness upon it, is in reality the fruit of Allah's mercy, compassion and guidance. Likewise, turning to Allah in this matter is in reality the fruit of the creed of Tawhid (Divine Oneness). Therefore, among the matters for which a believer seeks help and support from his Lord, the supplication for the ability to walk upon the straight path is an extremely important and great objective. The truth is that the happiness of this world and the Hereafter depends upon a person being guided to the straight course. And reaching the straight course is in reality reaching that Divine order (ilahi namus) which creates balance and harmony between the movement of this whole universe and the movement of this small human being within it, and which directs both of them towards Allah, the Lord of the worlds.

After this, the Exalted Lord explains the reality of that path: "The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have incurred (Your) wrath, nor of those who have gone astray." That is, the path of those for whom Allah's favour has been written in their destiny, and not the path of those who recognised the truth and then turned away from it, or those who were deprived of recognition of the path of truth from the very beginning and could not attain guidance. Rather, the path of those who are blessed and who have reached the truth is the path of those people.

In short, this is a brief surah, recited repeatedly in Salah, without which the Salah is not valid, and despite its brevity it contains the most important and fundamental beliefs of the Islamic view of life. Moreover, it gives those conscious guidances whose springs flow from the Islamic conception of life.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 1, verse 7:

﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have incurred (Your) wrath, nor of those who are astray.﴾

In Sahih Muslim, Hadrat Ala' narrates from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Allah the Exalted said: "I have divided the prayer (salah) between Myself and My servant into two equal halves. Half is for Me and half is for My servant, and My servant shall have whatever he asks for. When the servant says, ﴿Al-hamdu lillahi rabbil-'alamin﴾ (All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds), Allah the Exalted says, 'My servant has praised Me.' When he says, ﴿Ar-Rahmanir-Rahim﴾ (The Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate), Allah says, 'My servant has extolled Me.' When he says, ﴿Maliki yawmid-din﴾ (Master of the Day of Judgement), Allah says, 'My servant has glorified Me.' When he says, ﴿Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in﴾ (You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help), Allah says, 'This is shared between Me and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.' When he recites, ﴿Ihdinas-siratal-mustaqim … wa lad-dallin﴾ (Guide us to the straight path … nor of those who are astray), Allah says, 'This is for My servant, and he shall have what he has asked for.'"

In light of this explanation and commentary, the wisdom becomes clear behind why Allah has made it obligatory to recite this Surah in prayer at least seventeen times, and if someone recites it more than that, it is repeated even more times.
